sed -n '1,1400p' /Users/masterman/NLP/cloudcaptions/docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-20-exact-caption-style-copy-v1.md\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\"aggregated_output\\\\\\\":\\\\\\\"# Exact Caption Style Copy V1 Design\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Date:** 2026-07-20  \\\\\\\\n**Status:** Proposed for approval  \\\\\\\\n**Repository:** CloudCaptions, extending the existing admin Style Copy V3 workflow\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Goal\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nGiven a captioned image or video reference, CloudCap should identify the closest legally usable font face from a large server-side catalog, recover the visible face, outline, shadow, glow, background, and basic typography settings, render the proposed style through CloudCap's real layout and paint path, and let an admin inspect and accept the result without hand-tuning every field.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n“Exact visual match” is an evidence grade, not a claim about unknowable source metadata. CloudCap may label a result an exact visual match only when one immutable catalog face revision and the fitted style pass strict multi-sample visual gates. It may say “verified source font” only when trusted embedded metadata or user-supplied source font bytes prove identity. Otherwise it reports a very close or closest available match and shows the remaining differences.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Product Scope\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### North star\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nAny creator can supply a caption reference, receive a reproducible CloudCap style backed by a broad licensed font catalog, compare it against the source, correct uncertain fields, and save it to a personal or shared style library. The same selected font bytes render in editor preview, browser export, worker export, and Mac mini server rendering.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Current milestone\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThis V1 upgrades the existing admin-only Style Copy workflow and the shared font system end to end:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- synchronize the full Google Fonts catalog to persistent Mac mini storage;\\\\\\\\n- allow administrator imports of additional web-embeddable font files with explicit license metadata;\\\\\\\\n- expose the catalog in the existing editor font picker without loading thousands of font files;\\\\\\\\n- run local font retrieval, style fitting, and validation on the Mac mini;\\\\\\\\n- add the missing font-weight, font-style, outline, shadow, glow, and match-diagnostic fields to the style-copy contract;\\\\\\\\n- generate a real CloudCap preview video and reference comparison before acceptance;\\\\\\\\n- retain the existing durable job, event replay, retry, cancellation, and evidence cleanup behavior.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe V1 entry point stays in the admin Default Styles workflow. The server contracts remain target-neutral so a later user-facing entry point does not require a second matcher or persistence model.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Deliberate boundary\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n“Any available font” means any face CloudCap is authorized to store and serve as a webfont with stable bytes. V1 includes the full Google Fonts repository and administrator-imported fonts marked as web-embedding and redistribution permitted. It does not copy arbitrary macOS system fonts or crawl unknown font websites. A font that cannot legally and technically reach the browser cannot be an applicable match, because editor and export parity would be impossible.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Current Problems Being Fixed\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n1. The Rust `FontClassHint` is expressly a class hint, not a font identification, and the current analyzer often returns no `fontFamily`.\\\\\\\\n2. The TypeScript mapping contract carries an outline color but not outline thickness, and carries no standard shadow or glow parameters.\\\\\\\\n3. Font weight is reduced to a `bold` boolean, so 500, 600, 700, 800, and 900 faces cannot be distinguished faithfully.\\\\\\\\n4. Italic evidence exists in Rust but the production style model and canvas paint path do not consistently render a font style.\\\\\\\\n5. The current fidelity score merges face, outline, shadow, and glow into one foreground mask. A wrong face with a thick outline can therefore score well.\\\\\\\\n6. The checked-in picker has roughly thirty faces, while the headless Mac renderer registers only a smaller hard-coded subset.\\\\\\\\n7. The current Google Fonts CSS approach is suitable for a small list but not for thousands of faces. Loading or parsing one enormous CSS document would hurt page load, workers, and exports.\\\\\\\\n8. The existing Style Copy worker is not yet installed as a managed Mac mini production service.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## User Stories\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Primary journey\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n1. An admin opens Copy from Reference, uploads a reference through the existing direct-to-storage flow or supplies an allowed media URL, and starts analysis.\\\\\\\\n2. The run shows truthful stages: preparing media, extracting captions, separating text layers, searching fonts, fitting effects, validating, and rendering preview.\\\\\\\\n3. The review surface shows the selected face, immutable face revision, match grade, per-field confidence, top alternatives, source-versus-candidate comparison, warnings, and a real preview video.\\\\\\\\n4. The admin can adjust a proposed style with the existing style controls, rerun validation, and accept only after a current preview exists.\\\\\\\\n5. Acceptance stores an immutable style snapshot and font-face reference. The style remains renderable after raw reference crops expire.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Return and revisit\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- Reloading or returning to the run restores the current server snapshot, candidate list, top font alternatives, match artifacts, preview state, and event cursor.\\\\\\\\n- Catalog updates do not change an accepted result because accepted styles point to content-addressed font bytes.\\\\\\\\n- Expired raw evidence is visibly marked; accepted style, diagnostics, font license, and preview provenance remain.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Failure and recovery\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- Missing model artifacts, missing Segment, an invalid font catalog, unsafe media, low OCR confidence, unsupported glyphs, matcher timeout, renderer failure, lost worker lease, preview failure, and cleanup failure all produce typed errors and named events.\\\\\\\\n- Recoverable runs can be retried with a new run id linked to the original. The old result remains inspectable.\\\\\\\\n- Cancellation interrupts Segment, the Python matcher, its renderer child, and FFmpeg as one process group; temporary files are cleaned and the run becomes terminally cancelled.\\\\\\\\n- If the exact face is not in the usable catalog, the run still completes as `closest_available`; it never claims exactness.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Catalog journey\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- An operator can synchronize a pinned Google Fonts revision, inspect counts and rejected faces, import a licensed font, rebuild derived indexes, and run a health check from a CLI.\\\\\\\\n- The editor can search the server catalog by family, style, category, script, and weight. Only visible font specimens are lazily loaded.\\\\\\\\n- Selecting a catalog face updates the real caption style and layout. The same face bytes are supplied to preview and every export path.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Options Considered\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### A. Exhaustive production rendering of every face\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nRender every catalog face through the full CloudCap pipeline, then optimize effects for each one.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- Best theoretical direct comparison.\\\\\\\\n- Too slow and resource-heavy for thousands of faces.\\\\\\\\n- Repeated font registration and full layout/raster work would make the Mac mini queue It should help users find, understand, and change preferences with minimal chrome.\n\n## Defaults\n\n- Do not repeat the selected tab, sidebar item, or section name as a heading inside the panel.\n- Do not add subtitles that explain obvious groups.\n- Do not describe what visible controls already say.\n- Prefer compact rows: label, optional current value, control, validation or error when needed.\n- Add helper text only when it explains consequences, scope, persistence, sync, privacy, security, irreversible behavior, constraints, or ambiguous terminology.\n- Keep hierarchy shallow: tabs or sidebar sections at the top level, then grouped controls.\n- Avoid nested cards, decorative wrappers, intro copy, empty headings, and repeated \"Settings\" labels.\n- Use status text only for real state: unsaved changes, saving, saved, failed, unavailable, permission required.\n- Make save semantics explicit: auto-save, Apply/Cancel, or Save. Do not mix them casually.\n- Preserve the host platform or design-system conventions before inventing custom settings chrome.\n\n## Content Test\n\nBefore adding any heading, subtitle, description, icon, badge, or callout, ask:\n\n1. Would the user be confused without this text?\n2. Does it explain a consequence or boundary the control itself cannot show?\n3. Does it change what the user should do?\n\nIf all answers are no, delete it.\n\n## Persistence And Scope\n\nEvery meaningful setting still needs explicit behavior:\n\n- whether it persists,\n- where it is stored,\n- who owns it,\n- when it is loaded and saved,\n- whether it is local, workspace-level, account-level, or synced,\n- how reset, migration, and verification work.\n\nThis persistence design belongs in the plan or spec, not as explanatory prose inside the dialog unless the user needs it to make a safe choice.\n\n## Common Mistakes\n\n| Mistake | Better |\n|---|---|\n| Tab says \"Appearance\", panel title says \"Appearance\", subtitle says \"Customize how the app looks.\" | Use the tab label only. Show the controls. |\n| \"Notification settings let you control notifications.\" | Delete it. |\n| A card per setting with icon, title, subtitle, and repeated copy. | Use dense labeled rows unless the setting has complex consequences. |\n| \"Configure your editor preferences below.\" | Delete it. The dialog already provides the context. |\n| Helper text under every control for visual rhythm. | Add helper text only where it carries decision-critical information. |\n\n## Review Checklist\n\n- One clear navigation model.\n- No repeated tab or section titles.\n- No subtitles for self-explanatory sections.\n- No helper text that merely restates a label.\n- Controls are scannable without decorative cards.\n- Save, cancel, reset, and error behavior are visible when relevant.\n- Persistence and scope are designed, even when not narrated in the UI.\n"
  },

    "text": "---\nname: client-server-state-invariants\ndescription: Use for React server state, optimistic UI, caches, polling, streams, background jobs, persistence, or synchronization\n---\n\n# Client Server State Invariants\n\nReact bugs often expose deeper ownership mistakes. When several client, server, cache, stream, or persisted authorities can race or overwrite one another, make the relevant invariants explicit. A simple fetch-and-display path does not need the whole checklist.\n\n## Core Rule\n\nNo UI surface may treat data as authoritative unless the payload proves ownership, freshness, completeness, ordering, and terminal state.\n\nIf those words are missing from the plan, the plan is probably baking in a race condition.\n\n## Planning Checklist\n\nFor the cross-boundary state that can affect correctness, answer the applicable questions:\n\n1. **Owner:** What owns this state: server, client manager, URL, cache, stream, local storage, or worker/runtime?\n2. **Token:** What owner token protects async results: `requestId`, `runId`, `projectPath`, `operationId`, `workerId + seq`, or equivalent?\n3. **Provenance:** Is data server-authoritative, optimistic, cached preview, partial update, or historical fallback?\n4. **Completeness:** Does the payload declare what scope it is complete for? What may it erase?\n5. **Ordering:** What stable order is used: monotonic seq, `(createdAt, id)`, version, or cursor?\n6. **State machine:** What are the legal states, terminal states, and transitions?\n7. **Events:** Which server decisions are named events rather than client-side derivations?\n8. **Loading shape:** Which states are bootstrap, first load, incremental refresh, reconnect, resync, recovery, and terminal error?\n9. **Fallbacks:** Which legacy/fallback rows can render, and only after what authority is loaded?\n10. **Tests:** Which race, stale-response, event-sequence, reconnect, and merge tests prove the invariants?\n\n## Invariants To Require\n\n- Cached and optimistic data may pre-render, but cannot satisfy full-load gates.\n- Partial snapshots may add or refine state, but may not erase optimistic objects, delivered user input, read markers, or stream entries unless they declare complete scope.\n- Every async response checks that its owner token still matches before mutating visible state.\n- Mutation success handlers may navigate or clear UI only if they still own the current context, unless the action explicitly creates a new selected context.\n- Timers and polling callbacks re-check ownership immediately before acting.\n- Server decisions are emitted as named events; the client does not infer decisions by diffing snapshots.\n- SSE/WebSocket streams have event ids, replay/resume, and an explicit resync path.\n- Loading booleans are split by lifecycle stage. A leaf stream refresh must not unmount the whole page.\n- Append-only content has one writer, one reader, stable ids, and monotonic cursors.\n- Fallback DB rows or historical rows are gated behind stream loading and deduped by stable id plus safe equivalence.\n- Status classifiers distinguish active, runnable, blocked, awaiting user, terminal, stale, and recoverable states.\n- \"Latest\" queries have deterministic tie-breakers. Timestamp-only ordering is not enough.\n- Hot paths use bounded reads and do not synchronously load large bodies, bridge probes, schema setup, or heavy app graphs.\n- Process-local caches have explicit TTL/size bounds and invalidation rules.\n\n## Test Matrix\n\nPick the rows that match the work. Do not rely on one happy-path UI test.\n\n| Risk | Test shape |\n| --- | --- |\n| Stale async response | Start request A, switch owner, resolve A, assert it cannot mutate B |\n| Optimistic object erased | Create local optimistic state, apply stale/partial snapshot, assert object remains |\n| Cache masquerades as loaded | Hydrate cache preview, assert full-load gate waits for server authority |\n| Mutation steals navigation | Start mutation, switch selection, resolve mutation, assert focus stays put |\n| Timer/poll stale-fire | Use fake timers or deferred promises; callback must re-check owner before acting |\n| Snapshot merge erases stream | Apply partial snapshot missing known entries, assert entries/read markers remain |\n| Event stream gap | Bootstrap snapshot, emit events during disconnect, reconnect with last id, assert replay or resync |\n| Server decision invisible | Exercise the branch and assert a named event such as `action.blocked`, `request.rejected`, `gave_up`, or `error.surfaced` |\n| State classifier wrong | Table-test every status into active/runnable/terminal/recoverable buckets |\n| Fallback duplicates stream | Load fallback rows then stream entries, assert no duplicate or false chronology |\n| Hot path bloats | Assert snapshots carry cursors not bodies; route returns before DB/heavy imports when possible |\n| Timestamp tie | Insert equal timestamps, assert deterministic order by id/seq |\n| Context switch journey | If the user approves a high-risk browser journey, start work in A, switch to B before completion, return to both, and inspect visible ownership and status |\n| Background and return | If the user approves a high-risk browser journey, background the app while polling/streaming continues, return, and inspect freshness and continuity |\n\nUse headless HTTP/SSE tests for control-plane decisions and focused React/unit tests for Manager merging and ownership guards. For ordinary UI behavior, reproduce the affected interaction directly. Use `agentic-user-journey-testing` for a high-risk composed browser sequence only after explicit user approval. Do not ask a DOM test alone to prove a server decision.\n\n## Avoid These Shapes\n\n- one `isLoading` boolean for bootstrap, refresh, reconnect, and recovery;\n- cache or optimistic data treated as authoritative without provenance;\n- async callbacks that mutate state without checking owner tokens;\n- client-side derivation of server decisions;\n- snapshot diffs used as the only way to know what happened;\n- event streams without ids or resume;\n- timestamp-only \"latest\" queries;\n- parallel transcript or persistence surfaces that the frontend must reconcile;\n- unbounded process caches introduced to hide slow storage;\n- tests that prove only the DOM result when the bug is a server decision.\n\n## Review Prompt\n\nAsk this before implementation starts:\n\n> What can arrive late, out of order, partially, twice, or after the user changes context, and what test proves it cannot corrupt visible state?\n"

Load focused skills for focused problems instead of repeating their checklists here.\n\n## Route Specialized Work\n\n- New screens, forms, or major surfaces: `start-from-blocks`.\n- Server state, caches, polling, streams, optimistic UI, persistence, or background jobs: `client-server-state-invariants`.\n- Load, compilation, hydration, bundles, or import bloat: `optimizing-react-next-apps`.\n- Settings and preferences surfaces: `designing-settings-dialogs`.\n- Internationalization: `implementing-react-i18n` only when the user asks or the project already supports multiple languages.\n\nSmall visual changes to an existing UI—shape, size, position, spacing, color, typography, or copy—do not trigger these broader workflows unless the change actually crosses one of their boundaries.\n\n## State Ownership\n\nFor shared application state and app data structures, use global single-source-of-truth Manager classes unless the existing architecture has an equivalent owner. Components subscribe to the smallest slice they need and send intent through Manager methods.\n\nKeep local, high-churn presentation state local when it has no shared meaning: hover, open state, draft text, cursor position, and transient animation state do not need global ownership merely for consistency.\n\nAvoid broad root subscriptions to high-churn Manager snapshots. If typing or pointer movement repaints the app shell, narrow the subscription.\n\nPrefer explicit event handlers and Manager methods over effects that mirror one state value into another. Use effects for genuine synchronization with external systems or browser lifecycle.\n\nEvery async result that can update visible shared state should confirm it still belongs to the active request, route, or entity before committing its result.\n\n## Routing, Modules, and Configuration\n\n- Use framework-native routing where it is the framework's normal model; otherwise prefer explicit routes.\n- Use ES module `import`, not `require()`.\n- Use `pnpm` and `pnpm dlx`, never `npm` or `npx`.\n- Keep reviewable frontend strings and settings in source or JSON, not `.env`.\n- Preserve server rendering when it provides useful initial HTML. Do not push an entire route behind `\"use client\"` without a concrete need.\n- Lazy-load genuinely rare or route-conditional heavy surfaces; measure bundle impact instead of assuming an import is expensive.\n\n## UI Components\n\nUse the project's design system. In this fork, new app surfaces default to `shadcn/ui`; use its existing primitive before hand-building a control. Dropdown action menus use ShadCN Dropdown Menu, while Select, Command/Combobox, and Context Menu are used for their matching interactions.\n\nDo not re-run a block search for a cosmetic edit to an existing element.\n\n## Verification\n\n- Pure visual changes: inspect the affected desktop and mobile viewports. Do not add automated tests.\n- Ordinary component behavior: perform the affected interaction and run existing relevant checks; new tests are optional unless the user requests them or a real regression risk justifies them.\n- Database, data, API, persistence, or contract behavior: use `test-driven-development`.\n- High-risk multi-step UI journeys: consider `agentic-user-journey-testing`, but do not run it without explicit user approval.\n\nNever invent timing thresholds for rendering, hydration, or CLI calls. Measure the real application or command when performance is part of the request.\n"

    "text": "---\nname: implementing-react-i18n\ndescription: Use for React translations, locale resources, language selectors, or stale UI after locale changes\n---\n\n# Implementing React I18n\n\n## Overview\n\nUse the shared i18n library as the source of truth: locale state lives in an `i18nManager`, user-facing strings live in locale JSON resources, call sites render through `t(\"key\", params?)`, and React components subscribe only so language changes repaint.\n\n## First Product Question\n\nWhen building a meaningful React UI and the user has not mentioned language support, offer it as an option:\n\n> Should we support other languages? If yes, I will wire user-facing copy through i18n resources now instead of hardcoding strings.\n\nIf the user says yes, asks for language support, mentions locale/i18n/translation, or reports that language switching only updates part of the UI, use this skill.\n\n## Required Pattern\n\n1. Create or reuse `shared/locales/*.json` as flat dotted-key resources.\n2. Create or reuse `src/lib/i18n.ts` with:\n   - `i18nManager = createI18nManager(...)`\n   - `export const t = i18nManager.t`\n   - `export function useI18nSnapshot()` using `useSyncExternalStore`\n   - dynamic locale loaders for non-fallback languages\n3. Components that render translated text call `useI18nSnapshot()` and render with `t(...)`.\n4. Non-React modules use `t(...)` where user-visible text is produced.\n5. Store stable ids and translate at render time. Do not persist translated UI copy.\n\n```ts\nimport { useCallback, useSyncExternalStore } from \"react\";\nimport { createI18nManager } from \"@danduma/i18n\";\nimport fallbackDictionary from \"../../shared/locales/en.json\";\n\nexport const localeLoaders = {\n  es: async () => (await import(\"../../shared/locales/es.json\")).default,\n} as const;\n\nexport const i18nManager = createI18nManager({\n  dictionaries: { en: fallbackDictionary },\n  localeLoaders,\n  fallbackLocale: \"en\",\n  storageKey: \"app-locale\",\n});\n\nexport const t = i18nManager.t;\n\nexport function useI18nSnapshot() {\n  return useSyncExternalStore(\n    useCallback((listener) => i18nManager.subscribe(listener), []),\n    useCallback(() => i18nManager.getSnapshot(), []),\n    () => i18nManager.getSnapshot(),\n  );\n}\n```\n\n```tsx\nimport { t, useI18nSnapshot } from \"@/lib/i18n\";\n\nexport function SaveButton() {\n  useI18nSnapshot();\n\n  return <button type=\"button\">{t(\"common.save\")}</button>;\n}\n```\n\nThe hook is not the translation API. It exists to subscribe the component. The `t()` function is the translation API.\n\n## What Must Be Translated\n\nEvery user-facing frontend string must use `t()`:\n\n- JSX text, button labels, menu items, tab labels, empty states, status labels\n- `aria-label`, `title`, `placeholder`, `alt`, helper text, error fallback text\n- visible option labels for selects, segmented controls, toggles, and radio groups\n\nDo not translate protocol values, storage keys, API paths, CSS classes, model ids, database values, or enum values unless they are displayed as copy.\n\n## Locale Resource Rules\n\n- Add every new key to the fallback locale and every supported locale in the same change.\n- Add a parity test that compares all locale resource keys to the fallback dictionary.\n- Use stable dotted keys by surface and intent, for example `settings.runtime.recovery`.\n- Interpolate with named params: `t(\"settings.agents.toggleWorker\", { worker: label })`.\n- If translations are not approved yet, either support only the fallback language or ask which languages to support. Do not invent broad language support silently.\n\n## Variable Naming\n\nNever name variables with locale codes or locale-like names. Avoid `it`, `en`, `es`, `enUS`, `locIt`, `locEnUs`, or similar names, especially in tests where `it` can shadow the test function.\n\nUse role-based names instead:\n\n- `fallbackDictionary`\n- `candidateDictionary`\n- `localeDictionaries`\n- `resourcesByLocale`\n- `supportedLocaleCodes`\n\n## Common Mistakes\n\n| Mistake | Fix |\n| --- | --- |\n| Importing `t` and never subscribing | Call `useI18nSnapshot()` in every React component that renders translated strings. |\n| Returning `{ t }` from a custom hook | Keep `t()` as the direct call-site API; use hooks only for snapshots/subscriptions. |\n| Translating only the language selector | Migrate the parent dialog, tabs, labels, placeholders, controls, and error fallbacks too. |\n| Using localized labels as state | Store stable ids like `queue`; render `t(\"settings.runtime.queue\")`. |\n| Adding English keys only | Update every supported locale and run the key parity test. |\n\n## Verification\n\nRun focused checks after any i18n change:\n\n```bash\npnpm test tests/lib/i18n.test.ts\npnpm test tests/ui/settings-dialog.test.ts\npnpm exec tsc --noEmit\n```\n\nFor broader migrations, also run relevant UI tests and a browser smoke test: change language, reload, and verify representative labels outside the language selector update.\n"

    "text": "# Lifecycle Observability & Resilience Testing\n\n> What we keep getting wrong, why our tests don't catch it, and the discipline that fixes it.\n\nRelated: `docs/architecture/hot-path-responsiveness-and-resource-leaks.md`\ndocuments the May 2026 reload/worker-streaming latency incident and the\nresource-ownership rules for keeping page bootstrap, SSE, and worker stream\npaths responsive while agents are running.\n\n## Multi-runner client lifecycle\n\nEach saved runner profile owns one `RunnerConnection` state machine and at most\none main event stream. A registry starts every profile connection, not only the\nvisible one. Switching the visible workspace changes active managers/query\ncaches and terminal ownership without closing inactive main streams.\n\nEvery bootstrap, snapshot, frame, retry, timer, and mutation checks profile and\nlearned runner identity before applying state. Stored cursors include the\nrunner's stream epoch. `runner.stopping`, `auth.session_revoked`, and\n`stream.resync_required` are typed terminal/control outcomes, not generic\nnetwork failures.\n\nElectron, VS Code, and Capacitor host bridges have bounded stream delivery and\nmust cancel upstream work on overflow. Mobile suspension persists cursors,\ncloses streams, and reconnects on resume; it must not claim background\ndelivery. Platform lifecycle contract tests live under `tests/electron`,\n`tests/vscode`, `tests/mobile`, and `tests/runtime-api`; real two-runner and\neight-runner journeys live under `tests/e2e`.\n\n## Interactive protocol invariant\n\nAn advertised interactive agent capability is operational only when the complete user journey is implemented: receive the request, append it to the unified worker stream, render an actionable control in the main conversation, submit the exact protocol response, and append a terminal outcome before resolving the agent request. Side-panel-only controls do not satisfy this invariant. Every form shape and permission option emitted by a supported adapter must be covered by a finite wire-to-UI regression matrix.\n\nActionability comes only from the live runtime's `pendingElicitations` and\n`pendingPermissions`; an open worker-stream row proves only that a request\nexisted. After reattach or recreation, compare the durable open rows with the\nruntime-owned request ids and append terminal `cancelled` rows for any orphaned\nrequests before publishing the recovered worker. The UI may render the stream\nrows as history, but must never turn them back into response controls.\n\nRelated: `docs/architecture/timing-determinism-audit.md` records the May 20,\n2026 audit of race-prone frontend and control-plane patterns: cached snapshots\npretending to be authoritative, stale async callbacks, timer-owned actions,\ntimestamp-only ordering, and silent wake/lease contention.\n\n## Interrupted-turn recovery invariant\n\nReattaching a provider session restores conversation context; it does not prove\nthat the interrupted turn is running again. If a persisted active direct worker\nis missing after a runner restart and the reattached runtime comes back idle\nwithout a terminal stop reason or pending user input, recovery must explicitly\nsend a continuation prompt, keep the run `running`, and persist the eventual\nturn result. The continuation runs as an owned background conversation task so\nsnapshot bootstrap does not block on the agent turn. A newer user turn may\nsupersede it, but that decision must resolve the recovery incident and emit a\nnamed event.\n\nAn intentional stop or steer abort is a successful ownership handoff, not a\nworker failure. Older initial-turn handlers must recognize the abort and must\nnot emit `run_failed` or overwrite the replacement turn's status. Every queue\nrow claimed by the interrupted delivery must leave `delivering`: close it as\ndelivered if its exact message id reached the transcript, otherwise return it\nto pending. An elicitation answer resumes the turn that already owns the live\nquestion, so it must never wait behind that same turn's per-worker gate; doing\nso is a self-deadlock because the turn cannot finish until the answer arrives.\nA steer is also allowed to supersede a retry/edit recovery that owns the\nconversation mutex. It must first abort the registered recovery turn, then\nwait for the mutex and acknowledge the replacement without awaiting the new\nprovider turn. Otherwise the request inherits provider-turn latency and can\nexpire at an HTTP proxy even though the user's intent was to interrupt it.\n\n## Provider identity and startup ownership invariant\n\nA requested provider model id and the provider's reported session value are\ndifferent namespaces. Exact string equality is not an identity check: an ACP\nadapter may report a provider alias such as `opus[1m]` for the canonical\n`claude-opus-5` request. Accept an alias only when one model-menu entry\nunambiguously proves the same family and version; empty, missing, duplicated,\ninternally contradictory, cross-family, or cross-version evidence refuses the launch.\nPersist canonical requested intent separately from observed effective identity.\n\nThe launch scope owns every child, runtime client, and temporary skill link\nuntil the fully constructed agent record is inserted into the manager registry.\nThat insertion is the ownership transfer. Any earlier rejection, timeout, or\nabort must settle cleanup before returning the original error. Cleanup failures\nare surfaced without replacing that primary failure. A pool transfer succeeds\nonly when the pool explicitly accepts ownership, and a checked-out pool member\nmust be owned before the next failure-prone await.\n\nExpected transport teardown is cancellation, not a process error. In\nparticular, closing a compressed HTTP/SSE response must cancel and settle both\nthe upstream reader and gzip consumer without destroying zlib with a synthetic\nclient-disconnect error. Unexpected compression failures still propagate to the\nserver error boundary.\n\nA persisted `lost` worker is durable non-health evidence even though it is not\nan active worker status. With no matching live agent it must classify as\nrecovery-required, remain out of the `running` projection, and retain one\nunsettled incident across selected and background syncs. The incident identity\ncheck and insertion occur under one SQLite write transaction so concurrent\nrecovery sources cannot duplicate it. Only verified active work or a terminal\nrun may resolve that incident.\n\n## Why this document exists\n\nOver a single afternoon we hit three production-class bugs that the existing test\nsuite did not catch and could not have caught:\n\n1. **Session fails to reconnect after a server restart and gives up after the\n   first attempt.** No user-visible message, no telemetry event, no recovery\n   incident — just a silently dead session.\n2. **`DELETE /conversations/:id` fails with a foreign-key constraint** because\n   related rows in dependent tables were not cleared first. The error surfaces\n   as an opaque 500.\n3. **Running plan-improvement agents fails because leftover state blocks the\n   new run.** The block is silent; the user sees nothing happen and assumes the\n   button is broken.\n\nThese are not unrelated bugs. They share a single root cause:\n\n> **The server makes state transitions that nobody observes.** Neither the user,\n> nor the UI, nor any test client can tell what the server decided. So bugs in\n> the *decision* (gave up too early, took the wrong branch, refused silently)\n> are invisible.\n\nThis document records what we learned and the rules we now follow so that this\nclass of bug stops shipping.\n\nRelated incident note: `docs/architecture/supervisor-worker-switching-incident.md`\nrecords the worker-switching failure from session `690d2fa9f2a7`, where\n`awaiting_user` was treated as runnable, Gemini workers were live but persisted\nas `starting`, and duplicate continuation workers were spawned.\n\nRelated direct-control note:\n`docs/architecture/direct-control-session-regressions.md` records the\n`ffb912d4d5d7`, `937e642f3535`, and `734cc38f4d7f` regressions around\nlifecycle noise, stale queued send-now state, missing unified-stream worker\noutput, and permanent \"Thinking...\" indicators.\n\nRelated state-staleness note:\n`docs/architecture/state-staleness-and-session-lifecycle-lessons.md` records\nthe `0785684884fa`, `14260d2a2df0`, `ecea142f7344`, and `18fc406457f3`\nregressions around stale SSE/cache payloads, queued-message races, direct-run\nstatus classification, unread markers, and worker-stream loading.\n\n---\n\n## What we found in the audit\n\nA targeted audit of `src/app/api/events/route.ts` plus the planning, recovery,\nand bridge-client subsystems revealed the structural gaps.\n\n### 1. The SSE stream is a snapshot stream, not an event stream\n\n`/api/events` emits exactly one named event: `update`, whose payload is the\n*entire* current state of the world for the selected run (messages, plans,\nruns, workers, planItems, clarifications, executionEvents, supervisor\ninterventions, queued messages, recovery incidents, review runs/rounds/findings).\n\nThere are no other named events. An observer cannot ask \"did a worker spawn?\"\nor \"was a recovery attempted?\" — only \"is the state now different?\" To answer\nthe first kind of question the client must **diff snapshots**, which is:\n\n- **Ambiguous** — many transitions produce identical visible state (a worker\n  that was reattached and a worker that was recreated both end up as\n  `status=\"running\"`).\n- **Lossy** — fast transitions can be coalesced inside a single snapshot\n  interval and disappear entirely. (e.g. `starting → running → completed`\n  inside one 15s window.)\n- **Forced to re-derive server decisions** — the client has to reconstruct\n  *why* state changed, which requires duplicating server logic.\n\n### 2. There is no event ID and no resume\n\nThe SSE frames have no `id:` field. There is no `Last-Event-ID` handling on the\nserver. A client that disconnects and reconnects gets a fresh snapshot and has\n*no way to know* whether events fired during the gap. For chaos testing (where\nwe deliberately drop the connection) this is fatal — we cannot assert\n\"between t0 and t1 the server emitted [X, Y, Z]\" because the wire format does\nnot carry that information.\n\nThere is a `?snapshot=1` bootstrap endpoint, which is good. There is no\n\"give me the events I missed since id N\" endpoint, which is the gap.\n\n### 3. Several decisions are invisible to the wire\n\nConcrete state transitions that **the server makes** but **never tells anyone\nabout**:\n\n| Transition | Where it happens | Wire visibility |\n|---|---|---|\n| Worker spawned | `bridge-client/index.ts spawnAgent` | None — inferred from a row appearing |\n| Worker reattached vs recreated after restart | `restart-control.ts` / recovery path | **None** — both look like `status=\"running\"` |\n| Recovery gave up after N attempts | `recoveryIncidents.autoAttemptCount` increments | Partial — count is visible but there is no terminal \"abandoned\" state |\n| Plan readiness reached | `derivePlanningStatus()` — runs **client-side** | **None** — it is a client-side derivation, not a server event |\n| Plan-improvement blocked by leftover state | `planning/review.ts` early-return | **None** — silent refusal |\n| Conversation delete FK violation | `/api/conversations/[id]` DELETE | None as a typed event — only a 500 response |\n| Message ack / persisted / streaming chunk | `conversations/send-message.ts` | Partial — only the resulting queued-message status |\n\nEvery row in this table is a bug class waiting to ship. If the server can\nsilently decide \"I gave up\", \"I refused\", \"I took branch B not A\", and the\ntest harness has no way to assert which branch it took, the test harness is\nstructurally incapable of catching the bug.\n\n### 4. The user-facing surface mirrors the test-facing surface\n\nThe reason \"leftover state blocked the run\" did not show a user message is the\n**same reason** no test could detect it: there was no event for it. Make the\nstate transitions observable, and both the UI fix and the test coverage\nfollow. Conversely, if a transition is observable only by re-deriving from a\nsnapshot diff, both the UI and tests will be brittle in the same ways.\n\nThis is the central insight: **observability for users and observability for\ntests are the same problem**.\n\n### 5. Playwright e2e is the wrong layer for resilience\n\nThe existing `tests/e2e/*.spec.ts` files boot Chromium. They are slow (tens of\nseconds per scenario), flaky against real subprocess restarts, and they\nexercise UI rendering rather than control-plane decisions. The bugs we are\nhitting are not UI bugs — they are control-plane bugs. We should be hitting\nHTTP/SSE directly, in Node, with no browser. The UI is one consumer of the\ncontrol plane; the chaos harness is another.\n\n---\n\n## The rules we now follow\n\nThese are not suggestions. They are the discipline that makes this class of\nbug stop happening.\n\n### Rule 1: every server-side state transition emits a named event\n\nIf the server makes a decision — spawn, reattach, recreate, give up, refuse,\ndelete, fail — that decision is published on the event stream with a\n**named event type**, not just a state delta. Examples:\n\n- `worker.spawned`, `worker.status` (with `prev` and `next`), `worker.terminal`\n- `worker.reattached`, `worker.recreated`\n- `plan.ready`, `plan.review.started`, `plan.review.finished`,\n  `plan.review.blocked` (with a `reason`)\n- `recovery.opened`, `recovery.attempt`, `recovery.gave_up`, `recovery.resolved`\n- `conversation.deleted`, `conversation.delete_failed` (with FK details)\n- `error.surfaced` — the catch-all for anything the user should know about\n\n**Rule of thumb:** if a server method has an early-return, a try/catch that\nswallows, or a branch that depends on a state check, it emits an event.\n\"Silent\" is a code smell.\n\n### Rule 2: errors that affect the user are events, not just response codes\n\nA 500 with a body is not enough. A 200 that quietly did nothing is worse. Every\nuser-relevant failure publishes `error.surfaced` with a stable code, a\nhuman-readable message, and the relevant run/worker/conversation ids. The UI's\njob is to render `error.surfaced` events into toasts/banners. The test\nharness's job is to assert that the expected `error.surfaced` event fired.\n\nA failure that does not produce an `error.surfaced` event is a bug — even if\nthe underlying behaviour is technically correct — because it is invisible to\nthe user and to the tests.\n\nThe event carries the stable id of the subject that failed. Conversation and\nworker failures use `runId`, `conversationId`, or `workerId`; account-only\nsettings failures use `accountId` rather than pretending an account is a\nconversation.\n\n### Rule 3: the event stream is SSE-spec compliant\n\n- Every frame has an `id:` field. IDs are monotonic.\n- The server keeps a bounded **ring buffer** (≥ 500 entries) of recent events.\n- The server honours `Last-Event-ID` on reconnect: it replays everything after\n  that id from the buffer, then resumes live streaming.\n- If the requested id has fallen out of the buffer, the server emits a\n  `stream.resync_required` event so the client knows to re-bootstrap from\n  `?snapshot=1` rather than silently miss events.\n\nThis is the SSE spec. We were not following it. We are now.\n\n### Rule 4: named events alongside, not instead of, snapshots\n\nThe existing `update` snapshot event stays. The UI keeps consuming it. The new\nnamed events are *additional* frames on the same stream. Clients that don't\ncare about a given event type ignore it. There is no `?test=1` flag, no\nseparate test endpoint, no parallel surface that can drift.\n\nA new named event is not client-visible merely because the server emits it.\nIts regression test must prove the complete delivery chain: the EventSource\nadapter subscribes to the exact event name, the runtime stream normalizer\npreserves that name as `kind`, and the owning client manager dispatches the\nbounded payload. Test at least one real named frame through this chain; handler\nunit tests alone cannot detect an omitted subscription or a normalizer that\ndrops the event kind.\n\nA committed control-plane row proves durable intent, not delivery to an\nexternal worker or event consumer. Any post-commit side effect must have one\nordering owner, a durable delivery marker, a retry wake-up mechanism, startup\nrecovery, and a last-moment canonical fence. Idempotent request replay must\nresume unsettled delivery instead of returning stored success while skipping\nthe side effect. When a newer revision arrives during an in-flight call, the\nordered dispatcher must converge the external system to that newest revision\nbefore releasing the per-subject queue.\n\nIf a transition is worth emitting for tests, it is worth emitting in\nproduction. Anything else creates a second observability surface that will\ndiverge from reality.\n\n### Rule 5: chaos testing belongs in the client, not the server\n\nWe do **not** add fault-injection code paths to the server. We do not add a\n\"random failure\" mode. The server stays clean. Chaos lives in the test\nclient as middleware:\n\n- An SSE wrapper that can drop the connection on command.\n- A `fetch` wrapper that can fail a configurable percentage of requests.\n- A harness that can SIGKILL the spawned server process and restart it.\n\nFaults are seeded for reproducibility. Every failure has a seed; replaying\nthe seed reproduces the failure.\n\n### Rule 6: tests assert on event sequences, not on rendered state\n\nA scenario test reads like a transcript:\n\n```\nexpect(events).toHaveEmitted(\"worker.spawned\", { runId });\nexpect(events).toHaveEmitted(\"worker.status\", { next: \"running\" });\nchaos.killServer();\nchaos.restartServer();\nexpect(events).toHaveEmitted(\"worker.reattached\", { runId });\n// not \"worker.recreated\", not absence — explicitly reattached\n```\n\n### Rule 7: cleanup waits for server-owned background work\n\nLifecycle scenarios may call routes that intentionally return before a direct\nworker turn finishes. That is fine for product latency, but it is not fine for\ntest cleanup to delete `OMNIHARNESS_ROOT` while those server-owned tasks are\nstill writing worker JSONL, recovery rows, or named events.\n\nRequired shape:\n\n- Fire-and-forget direct/planning turns are registered as background\n  conversation tasks.\n- The lifecycle harness waits for registered background tasks before deleting\n  its temp root.\n- A timeout while waiting is a test failure, not harmless stderr after the test\n  already passed.\n- Do not paper over storage `ENOENT` from cleanup races by retrying file writes;\n  the ownership bug is untracked background work.\n\nProduction deletion follows the same ownership rule. A conversation delete\ninstalls a run-scoped deletion fence before cancelling workers or removing\nrows. Initial worker startup checks that fence both before and after spawn, so\na worker that finishes spawning during deletion is cancelled before its prompt\ncan run. The fence remains until every tracked background task for the run has\nsettled; a one-shot best-effort cancel is not sufficient.\n\nAsserting on rendered DOM state is the wrong granularity. We assert on the\nserver's *decisions*, which are now first-class events.\n\n"
